## Proof

Let $S = \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i^2$. We want $\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{k} X_i^2}{S}\right]$.

**Symmetry argument.** The random variables $X_1, \dots, X_n$ are iid standard normals, so the joint distribution is invariant under any permutation of the indices. Consequently, for any $i, j \in \{1,\dots,n\}$,

$$
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{X_i^2}{S}\right] = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{X_j^2}{S}\right].
$$

Let this common value be $m$. Summing over all $i = 1, \dots, n$:

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{X_i^2}{S}\right] = n \cdot m = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i^2}{S}\right] = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{S}{S}\right] = \mathbb{E}[1] = 1.
$$

Hence $m = \tfrac{1}{n}$, and by linearity of expectation,

$$
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{k} X_i^2}{S}\right] = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{X_i^2}{S}\right] = k \cdot \frac{1}{n} = \frac{k}{n}.
$$

$$
\boxed{\mathbb{E}[\|Y\|^2] = \dfrac{k}{n}}
$$
